newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH PM SAYS INTEREST RATE CUT HAS BEEN DISCUSSED.
newsitem.headline: CZECH PM SAYS INTEREST RATE CUT HAS BEEN DISCUSSED.

text.p: Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said on Saturday there have been discussions in recent days with the central bank on lowering interest rates as part of a package of measures to help jump start the ailing economy.

Speaking after a meeting with leading businessmen on the planned measures, expected to be announced on April 16, Klaus said the package would be bigger than originally expected, though he refused to give any details.

When asked if a rate cut was one of the planned measures, Klaus said: "We have naturally spoken about the possibility on this theme with the central bank Governor, the Finance Minister, and others in the past two or three weeks."
The Czech crown and interbank money markets have been very volatile in the runup to the measures, with many analysts predicting a rate cut could be in the cards.
On Thursday, Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik said the Czech National Bank (CNB) and the government had agreed to coordinate their economic policies.

Klaus and other government ministers have recently been critical of the central bank's moves last June to tighten monetary policy, saying that the resulting slowdown in inflation has not been worth the price of a weakening in economic growth.

The Czech constitution requires the central bank to remain independent, but government ministers can participate in CNB board meetings, and CNB Governor Josef Tosovsky routinely attends cabinet meetings.
After Saturday's meeting Klaus added the measures adopted would affect both the monetary and budgetary policies, banking, privatisation and foreign trade.

He said that while some will take effect immediately, others will require further work by the Finance Ministry and the rest will require altered legislation and therefore take more time to be implemented.

Last June the central bank hiked its key discount rate by one full percentage point to 10.5 percent, and implemented a series of measures incluing repo rate hikes and raising minimum reserve requirements to choke a burgeoning money supply and ease inflationary pressures.

The moves appear to be working, with the M2 money supply, which measures currency, demand deposits, time and savings deposits, and foreign currency deposits, easing to 7.8 percent in December from 20.2 percent in the same month of 1995.
On Tuesday the CSU said inflation fell to an all-time low of 6.8 percent, year-on-year in March.

The Czech economy has enjoyed several years of demand-led growth as industry imported technology and a sharp rise in wages provoked a consumer boom. But industrial and construction output have both declined for two consecutive months as the central bank moves continue to bite.
